paras: The lynching of Dave Spearman and Sam Fair was the killing of two young Black farm laborers by a crowd near Prosperity, Newberry County, South Carolina, on January 19, 1881. Accused of assaulting and killing Bessie Werts, a white farmer's daughter, they were taken from the town guard house; Spearman was shot at a pine tree before dawn, and Fair, wounded and recaptured, was hanged at midday. The story ran in papers across the country, and the Charleston News and Courier declared that the lynchers' action "needs no apology."

Werts, printed also as Wertz, was the daughter of William Werts, a farmer about two miles from Prosperity who employed both men. Spearman and Fair were each about 21 or 22; Spearman lived on the place with his wife, Fair with his mother nearby. According to the reports, Werts was attacked and killed on the evening of Monday, January 17, while walking home from her brother's house.

A coroner's jury met at Prosperity on January 18 before Trial Justice A. H. Wheeler. A News and Courier reporter wrote that after H. C. Moseley found a strand of wool and a hair on Fair's vest, Fair said Spearman had planned the assault but that he had refused to join in. Spearman denied this, and both men were put under guard in the guard house when the jury adjourned without a verdict at about 1 a.m.

Some time after 2 a.m. on January 19 a crowd broke open the guard house and took Spearman to the scene of the crime. There, by the reporter's account, he confessed and named Fair as the killer; some wanted to burn him alive, but he was tied to a pine and shot by "a dozen guns" at about 4 a.m. The crowd then shot Fair at the guard house and left him for dead.

Fair was found later that morning in bed at his mother's house with slight wounds and brought back to Prosperity. Wheeler and the jurors demanded the prisoner, but the crowd "rushed over Justice Wheeler" and hanged Fair at about 1 p.m. in a pine grove half a mile to a mile from town. The reports stressed that Black men took part, one climbing the tree to pass the rope over a limb. The Columbia Register correspondent counted 250 or 300 witnesses; the Chicago Times put the participants at five or six hundred, "many colored men and women" among them.

That day the coroner's jury found that Werts had been killed by Spearman and Fair, and she was buried before six to eight hundred mourners. The two men's bodies lay unburied for several days after the Black church nearby refused them its graveyard, until two Newberry men paid for Fair's burial. No report of an arrest or prosecution of any lynchers appears in the coverage.

A Charleston wire ran in the St. Paul Daily Globe as "Prompt Punishment of Her Assailants," and a Columbia Register special appeared on January 21 in the New York Sun, National Republican and Richmond Dispatch. South Carolina weeklies used headings such as "Diabolical Crime of Two Negroes" and "Crime in its Highest Stage," while a Chicago Times special ran in Ohio as "Ever Present Horror in the Great Negro Districts" and in Tennessee as "Swiftly Avenged."

The News and Courier's editorial, reprinted in the Edgefield Advertiser and the Newberry Herald, held that "burning at the stake or chopping the offender into mince-meat were not too much." The Abbeville Press and Banner called lynch law "our only protection" against courts that would not punish, and the Yorkville Enquirer wrote of "the negroes assisting in the vindication of right." In April the Pickens Sentinel cited "the two negro brutes at Prosperity" while disputing the Press and Banner's charge that South Carolina habitually lynched "weak and defenceless negroes."

The Charleston wire said both men confessed; the Columbia Register correspondent said Fair admitted only knowing of the plan; the News and Courier reporter wrote that Spearman confessed only after the crowd took him to the scene. Accounts also differ on whether Fair was left for dead or escaped while running, and on whether the body was found by Fair or by farm laborers.

reader.title: Lynching of Dave Spearman and Sam Fair
bases: A crowd took two Black prisoners from the Prosperity guard house, shot one at a pine tree and hanged the other, over the objection of the trial justice (A9, A15, A2).

Spearman was shot by 'a dozen guns' and Fair hanged by a crowd of hundreds after they were taken from a guard house and from the trial justice, who demanded the prisoner (A15, A9, A13). The crowd acted on the accusation of rape and murder, and editors defended it as justice the courts would not give (A11, A7).

A Charleston wire, a Columbia Register special, News and Courier dispatches and a Chicago Times special agree on the guard house break, the shooting of Spearman and the hanging of Fair (A1, A2, A9, A12, A15).

accounts.label: Charleston wire
accounts.gist: Both men confessed; a large body of men took them out; Spearman was shot at the scene, while Fair escaped and was recaptured and hanged next day by 'a crowd of whites and blacks'.

accounts.label: Columbia Register correspondent at Prosperity
accounts.gist: Fair admitted only knowing of the plan; the crowd took Spearman to the scene, where 'it is said' he confessed, shot him, then shot Fair at the guard house and left him for dead; Fair was found at his mother's and hanged at 1 p.m. before 250-300 men.

accounts.label: News and Courier reporter at Prosperity
accounts.gist: Spearman denied Fair's statement at the inquest; the crowd took Spearman alone, heard his confession at the pine and shot him at 4 a.m., then shot Fair in the guard house; Fair slipped away, was recaptured and hanged in a pine grove at midday, a Black man passing the rope over the limb.

accounts.label: Chicago Times special from Newberry
accounts.gist: The body was found by farm laborers in a thicket; five or six hundred took part in Fair's hanging, many of them Black men and women; other Black men were said to be implicated.

South Carolina weeklies headlined 'Diabolical Crime of Two Negroes' and 'Crime in its Highest Stage' and called the hanging 'the vindication of right'.
Northern papers ran the wire and specials as 'Prompt Punishment of Her Assailants', 'That South Carolina Lynching', 'Swiftly Avenged' and 'Ever Present Horror in the Great Negro Districts'.

record_check.dossier: Widely reported double lynching of Dave Spearman and Sam Fair on January 19, 1881, taken from the Prosperity guard house

info: Spearman was taken from the guard house after 2 a.m. and shot about 4 a.m. on Wednesday, January 19, 1881 (reported in the first dispatches as Tuesday night, January 18); Fair was hanged about 1 p.m. the same day.

Spearman at the pine tree beside the path where the alleged crime took place, near the Werts farm two miles from Prosperity; Fair in a pine grove half a mile (or about one mile) from Prosperity, 'the suburbs of the town'.
Dave (David) Spearman and Sam Fair, Black farm laborers on the Werts place, each about 21 or 22; Spearman described as 'coal black', Fair as 'a mulatto'.
Accused of assaulting and killing Bessie Werts (also Wertz), daughter of William Werts, on the evening of Monday, January 17, 1881; the coroner's jury found she was killed by them.
A crowd of local men, white and Black; the News and Courier reporter described 'a mass of men, among whom were a number of negroes'.
The bodies lay unburied several days; the Chicago Times said two or three other Black men were said to be implicated and would meet the same 'justice' if the crowd believed them guilty.
